summary: Hebrew joins clauses without ever changing their word order: a subordinate clause looks exactly like a main clause — there is no verb-final rule as in German. Two kinds of linking words do the work. Separate words: וְ “and” (a prefix), אוֹ “or”, אֲבָל “but”, כִּי “because” (+ a clause; בִּגְלַל + a noun), לָכֵן “so, therefore” and, in speech, אָז “so”, וְאָז / אַחַר כָּךְ “and then”, אִם “if”. And the prefix שֶׁ “that”, written onto the first word of its clause: אֲנִי שָׂמֵחַ שֶׁאַתָּה פֹּה “I’m glad that you are here” — it is never left out, and it doubles the next letter when it can (שֶׁזֶּה, שֶׁלֹּא), but not before א ה ח ע ר. שֶׁ is the key to a whole family: a preposition + שֶׁ becomes a conjunction — כְּשֶׁ “when” (from כְּ “as”), לִפְנֵי שֶׁ “before”, אַחֲרֵי שֶׁ “after”, עַד שֶׁ “until”, מִשּׁוּם שֶׁ “because”, לַמְרוֹת שֶׁ and אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁ “although”. A clause can come first or second; when the subordinate clause comes first, a comma follows it: כְּשֶׁאֲנִי עָיֵף, אֲנִי שׁוֹתֶה קָפֶה. Two tense rules matter: after כְּשֶׁ and אִם a future event is in the future tense (כְּשֶׁאֶהְיֶה גָּדוֹל “when I grow up”, אִם יֵרֵד גֶּשֶׁם “if it rains”), and reported speech keeps the original tense.

blocks.caption: The word order inside both clauses stays subject – verb – object.

head: preposition
+ שֶׁ = conjunction
blocks.caption: The prepositions of lessons 11–15 become conjunctions with שֶׁ: לִפְנֵי הָעֲבוֹדָה “before work” → לִפְנֵי שֶׁאֲנִי הוֹלֵךְ “before I go”.

items.title: German
points: weil, dass, wenn, obwohl send the verb to the end: …, weil ich müde bin
deshalb takes first place, the verb follows: deshalb bleibe ich

items.title: Hebrew
points: nothing moves: כִּי אֲנִי עָיֵף “because I am tired”
לָכֵן אֲנִי נִשְׁאָר — the same order as without it

blocks.title: שֶׁ is written onto the next word
blocks.text: שֶׁאַתָּה, שֶׁהוּא, שֶׁהַבַּיִת, כְּשֶׁאֲנִי. In a phrase of several words only the last part takes it: לַמְרוֹת שֶׁהוּא, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהוּא. Before a letter that can be doubled it adds a dot: שֶׁזֶּה, שֶׁלֹּא, שֶׁכָּל.

blocks.title: Future after “when” and “if”
blocks.text: A future event after כְּשֶׁ or אִם is in the future tense: כְּשֶׁאֶהְיֶה גָּדוֹל, אִם יֵרֵד גֶּשֶׁם. (A general truth stays in the present: כְּשֶׁאֲנִי עָיֵף, אֲנִי שׁוֹתֶה קָפֶה “whenever I’m tired”.)

blocks.title: Sound-alikes
blocks.text: אִם “if” and עִם “with” are both pronounced im; כִּי “because” is a word, כְּ “like” a prefix; מָתַי? “when?” asks, כְּשֶׁ “when” joins.

blocks.caption: Y כִּי X “Y because X” — X, לָכֵן Y “X, so Y”: the same two facts, in either order.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when you join two clauses
questions: Is it “and / or / but”? → וְ / אוֹ / אֲבָל between them.
A reason or a result? → כִּי before the reason, לָכֵן (spoken אָז) before the result.
Time, condition, “that”, “although”? → כְּשֶׁ, אִם, שֶׁ, לַמְרוֹת שֶׁ — the prefixes go onto the next word.

askYourself: Just adding, choosing or contrasting? → וְ, אוֹ, אֲבָל (after a negative: אֶלָּא).
Giving the reason? → כִּי + clause (בִּגְלַל + noun); formal מִשּׁוּם שֶׁ.
Giving the result? → לָכֵן (spoken אָז) at the start of the result clause.
Next in time? → וְאָז / אַחַר כָּךְ.
When? → כְּשֶׁ written onto the next word; future event → future tense.
If? → אִם; future event → future tense.
That …? → שֶׁ on the next word — never leave it out.
Although? → לַמְרוֹת שֶׁ / אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁ; despite + noun → לַמְרוֹת.
Word order? → the same as in a main clause.
steps: Decide the relation (adding, contrast, cause, result, time, condition, content, concession).
Attach שֶׁ / כְּשֶׁ to the next word; keep normal word order; comma after a fronted subordinate clause.

traps: *אֲנִי יוֹדֵעַ הוּא פֹּה (no “that”) → אֲנִי יוֹדֵעַ שֶׁהוּא פֹּה.
*כִּי הַגֶּשֶׁם → בִּגְלַל הַגֶּשֶׁם (כִּי needs a clause).
*לָכֵן נִשְׁאָר אֲנִי (German order) → לָכֵן אֲנִי נִשְׁאָר.
*לֹא קָפֶה אֲבָל תֵּה → לֹא קָפֶה אֶלָּא תֵּה.
*אִם הוּא בָּא מָחָר for a future event → אִם הוּא יָבוֹא מָחָר.

quiz.why: שֶׁ is never left out, and it is written onto the next word.
כִּי needs a whole clause; before a noun use בִּגְלַל.

quiz.q: “I’m tired, so I’m staying at home”:
options: אֲנִי עָיֵף, לָכֵן אֲנִי נִשְׁאָר בַּבַּיִת.
אֲנִי עָיֵף, לָכֵן נִשְׁאָר אֲנִי בַּבַּיִת.
אֲנִי עָיֵף, כִּי אֲנִי נִשְׁאָר בַּבַּיִת.
quiz.answer: אֲנִי עָיֵף, לָכֵן אֲנִי נִשְׁאָר בַּבַּיִת.
quiz.why: לָכֵן introduces the result and the word order does not change (unlike German deshalb).
מָתַי only asks “when?”; כְּשֶׁ joins clauses.
Before a clause לַמְרוֹת needs שֶׁ.
After a negative, “but rather” is אֶלָּא.

quiz.q: In a Hebrew subordinate clause the verb …
options: stays where it is in a main clause
goes to the end, as in German
quiz.answer: stays where it is in a main clause
quiz.why: Hebrew has no verb-final rule: כִּי אֲנִי עָיֵף, שֶׁהוּא בָּא.

options: sound the same (im) but mean “if” and “with”
quiz.answer: sound the same (im) but mean “if” and “with”
quiz.why: Learn them apart by the first letter: א־ for “if”, ע־ for “with”.

seeAlso.note: Arabic has the same kind of “that” — أَنَّ, also inside لِأَنَّ “because” — but it must be followed by a noun in the accusative or a pronoun suffix (لِأَنَّهُ مُتْعَبٌ); Hebrew שֶׁ / כִּי take a plain clause. إِذَا “if”, عِنْدَمَا “when”, لِذٰلِكَ “so”, لٰكِنَّ “but”.

German weil, dass, wenn, obwohl send the verb to the end and deshalb pulls it forward; the Hebrew clause never changes its order. dass = שֶׁ, weil = כִּי, wenn / als = כְּשֶׁ, obwohl = לַמְרוֹת שֶׁ, deshalb = לָכֵן.
Chinese likes pairs — 因为 … 所以 … (because … so …), 虽然 … 但是 … (although … but …) — where Hebrew uses one word; and it has no word for “that” (我知道他是老师), where Hebrew cannot do without שֶׁ.

notes.text: Greek ότι / που ~ שֶׁ, όταν ~ כְּשֶׁ, αν ~ אִם, γιατί ~ כִּי, αλλά ~ אֲבָל, and the word order stays as in a main clause — as in Hebrew.

что ~ שֶׁ, когда ~ כְּשֶׁ, если ~ אִם, потому что ~ כִּי, но ~ אֲבָל; Russian also uses the future after когда / если for a future event (когда я вырасту ~ כְּשֶׁאֶהְיֶה גָּדוֹל). Hebrew שֶׁ is never left out.

que ~ שֶׁ, cuando ~ כְּשֶׁ, si ~ אִם, porque ~ כִּי, pero ~ אֲבָל. Where Spanish puts cuando + subjunctive (cuando sea grande), Hebrew uses the future: כְּשֶׁאֶהְיֶה גָּדוֹל. Like que, שֶׁ is never left out.

“That” can be left out in English, שֶׁ never: אֲנִי יוֹדֵעַ שֶׁהוּא פֹּה. After “when” and “if” English uses the present for the future (“when I grow up”); Hebrew uses the future: כְּשֶׁאֶהְיֶה גָּדוֹל, אִם יֵרֵד גֶּשֶׁם.

que ~ שֶׁ (never left out in either language), quand ~ כְּשֶׁ, si ~ אִם, parce que ~ כִּי, mais ~ אֲבָל. As with quand + future (quand je serai grand), Hebrew uses the future after כְּשֶׁ — and after אִם too, where French says s’il pleut.
weil, dass, wenn send the verb to the end; כִּי, שֶׁ, כְּשֶׁ change nothing. deshalb puts the verb before the subject; לָכֵן does not: לָכֵן אֲנִי נִשְׁאָר.
Hindi कि ~ שֶׁ, जब ~ כְּשֶׁ, अगर ~ אִם, क्योंकि ~ כִּי, लेकिन ~ אֲבָל; but Hindi keeps the verb at the end of each clause, while Hebrew keeps subject – verb – object.
Persian که ~ שֶׁ, وقتی که ~ כְּשֶׁ, اگر ~ אִם, چون ~ כִּי, ولی / اما ~ אֲבָל; but Persian keeps the verb at the end of each clause, Hebrew keeps subject – verb – object.
Marathi की “that”, जेव्हा “when”, जर “if”, कारण “because” are close to שֶׁ, כְּשֶׁ, אִם, כִּי; but Marathi keeps the verb at the end of each clause, and Hebrew needs no second word like तेव्हा / तर.
Arabic أَنَّ ~ שֶׁ, عِنْدَمَا ~ כְּשֶׁ, إِذَا / إِنْ ~ אִם, لِأَنَّ ~ כִּי, لٰكِنْ ~ אֲבָל, لِذٰلِكَ ~ לָכֵן. Written Arabic often puts the verb first; Hebrew keeps the subject first in both clauses.

Turkish builds subordinate clauses with verb forms (geldiğinde “when he comes”, geldiği için “because he came”); Hebrew uses linking words and leaves the verb as it is: כְּשֶׁהוּא בָּא, כִּי הוּא בָּא.
Japanese chains clauses with verb forms (-て, -たら, -から) placed at the end of the clause; Hebrew puts the linking word first (כִּי, כְּשֶׁ, אִם) and changes nothing in the verb.
Korean joins clauses with endings on the verb (-고, -아서, -면); Hebrew puts a separate linking word before the clause: וְ, כִּי, אִם.
Finnish että ~ שֶׁ, kun ~ כְּשֶׁ, jos ~ אִם, koska ~ כִּי, mutta ~ אֲבָל — linking words at the start, and the word order stays as in a main clause.
Hungarian hogy ~ שֶׁ, amikor ~ כְּשֶׁ, ha ~ אִם, mert ~ כִּי, de ~ אֲבָל — joining words at the start of the clause, as in Hebrew.
Swahili kwamba ~ שֶׁ, kwa sababu ~ כִּי, lakini ~ אֲבָל, kama ~ אִם — linking words before the clause with no change of order, as in Hebrew.
因为 ~ כִּי, 所以 ~ לָכֵן, 但是 ~ אֲבָל, 如果 ~ אִם; Chinese often pairs 因为 … 所以 …, Hebrew uses one of them. Chinese …的时候 “when” closes its clause; Hebrew כְּשֶׁ opens it.
vì ~ כִּי, nên ~ לָכֵן, nhưng ~ אֲבָל, nếu ~ אִם, khi ~ כְּשֶׁ — linking words at the start, as in Hebrew; Vietnamese often pairs vì … nên, Hebrew uses one of them.
Inuktitut joins clauses with verb moods (endings meaning “because”, “when”, “if”) rather than separate words; Hebrew uses linking words — כִּי, כְּשֶׁ, אִם — and changes nothing in the verb.
